Every month, algorithms identify a high-frequency problem in the data and bring it to the attention of a municipal department. Three levels of government work together. The goal is not to resolve a single case, but to address an entire category of problems.

Yet technology alone cannot govern a city.

Volunteer "lane managers" walk the alleys, spotting problems before they grow. Residents, businesses and community workers all become part of the early-warning system, providing eyes and ears that no algorithm can replace.

candidates.raw_excerpt: Astrolight has reached a key technology milestone as it looks to bring laser communications more into the satellite mainstream. For the first time, it established end-to-end optical communication links from its ATLAS-1 laser communication terminal in orbit to its OGS-2.5 optical ground station in Greece. Astrolight announced the demonstration on Oct. 8, in which the link moved from first light to routine operations at 1 Gbps within a week. The company developed the terminal working with the European Space Agency and worked with the Department of Aerospace of the University of Athens, and the Department of Physics of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki on this project. In the demonstration, Astrolight’s ATLAS-1 laser communication terminal on the ERMIS-3 a nanosatellite connected with the with HolOGS-1 optical ground station in Holomondas, Greece. Astrolight upgraded the ground station to its OGS-2.5 model for the PeakSat mission. Astrolight’s team in Lithuania has operated both systems remotely. candidates.title: China's FAST telescope finds rare triple-star system still evolving
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Chinese astronomers have found a rare evolving triple-star system involving a pulsar, using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope (FAST). 

The system, called J0435+3233, gives astronomers a natural lab to study how stars evolve and pull on each other, and test fundamental theories of gravity, including the strong equivalence principle. Its discovery also shows the value of combining observations across different wavelengths. The findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters on Friday.

Scientists believe all three stars formed from the same cloud of gas and dust. The heaviest exploded and became the pulsar. The second evolved into a white dwarf. The lightest survived both stages and is still evolving. Eventually, it too will become a white dwarf, leaving a stable system with one pulsar and two white dwarfs.

A pulsar is a fast-spinning neutron star that fires beams of radio waves. Analyzing five years of FAST observations, scientists found this one spins once every 3.2 milliseconds and orbits a white dwarf – the dense core of a dead star – once every eight days.

Researchers combined the radio data with publicly available infrared, optical and gamma-ray data to identify a third star, with a mass similar to the Sun's. It orbits the inner pulsar-white dwarf binary once every 73.5 years on an elongated path.

The third star also explains a strange FAST reading: the pulsar's spin period is increasing by about one nanosecond a year, roughly 100 times faster than comparable pulsars. The pull of the distant companion is behind this change.

candidates.title: SpaceX Moves to Acquire Nationwide Low-Band Spectrum for Starlink Mobile
candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX announced a deal Thursday afternoon to acquire nationwide, low-band spectrum from Grain Management to improve service for Starlink Mobile and enable the service to operate indoors. SpaceX and Grain Management said SpaceX will acquire 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band. The deal is subject to FCC approval. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. This comes just after the FCC approved SpaceX to deploy 15,000 satellites for its Starlink Mobile direct-to-device constellation. SpaceX explained how this spectrum will complement the service in a statement: “While Starlink Mobile’s global 2 GHz mid-band spectrum will provide high-bandwidth capacity in the United States, this new low-band spectrum will provide a coverage layer that ensures Starlink Mobile’s signal penetrates through obstacles, such as walls, and can provide service to customers’ devices even when they are in buildings,” SpaceX said. Grain is a private investment firm that acquired the block of spectrum from T-Mobile in a deal announced in early 2025 and just completed in August for $2.9 billion in cash and additional spectrum licenses. The spectrum’s “propagation characteristics make it well-suited for a broad range of mission-critical applications, including private wireless networks for electric utilities and other critical infrastructure operators, enterprise communications, and next-generation direct-to-device (D2D) satellite services,” Grain said in a recent statement. SpaceX also stated that most existing mobile devices already support this spectrum band. With this spectrum and the second-generation of Starlink Mobile satellites, SpaceX said Starlink Mobile will be “the first network operator to deploy both satellite and terrestrial spectrum,” and the network will provide “reliable service indoors, outdoors, in cellular dead zones, and everywhere in between.” Starlink Mobile, the direct-to-device constellation, is separate from SpaceX’s broadband internet constellation.

candidates.raw_excerpt: Margaret Hamilton, who coined the term "software engineering" and led the development of onboard flight software for NASA's Apollo program in the 1960s, died last week at the age of 90. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” said Olivier de Weck , interim head of the MIT Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics. “The Apollo program still stands as one of our greatest testaments to the power of collaboration, ingenuity, and engineering, and Hamilton was a fundamental contributor to that program’s success.” Born in 1936 in Paoli, Indiana, Hamilton graduated from Earlham College in 1958 with a degree in mathematics and a minor in philosophy—the latter a nod to her father (a poet) and grandfather (a headmaster). She married her first husband, James Cox Hamilton, that same year. candidates.title: Don’t Want to Spend Time With Your Kids? Train an AI Voice Model of Yourself to Read Them Bedtime Stories
candidates.raw_excerpt: Parenting is hard. Why not let an AI model take over some of your childrearing duties? It may come at the expense of forming lasting emotional bonds with your progeny, but that’s a tradeoff that some AI adherents, evidently, have calculated to be worth it. OpenAI Sam Altman has bragged about how much he relies on ChatGPT to raise his son, and also thinks it’s a good idea to let an AI-generated podcast replace the “so how’d your day go?” catchup talk a mom or dad has in the car when they pick their kid up from school. Altman’s comments were ruthlessly — and rightfully — mocked at the time. But his robo-rearing ideas pale in comparison to this latest take from an AI bro. In a now deleted post on X, Alvin Sng, a software engineer at the startup Factory AI, recalled a conversation he had with his wife when she asked him to read his newborn baby a book. As he explained, he had a better idea that required zero effort on his part. “I can just play an audiobook from my phone,” he told her. His spouse reasonably complained that an audiobook wouldn’t be in his voice. But Sng wasn’t to be outdone in the zero-effort-parenting department. “I can train a voice model,” he countered, before addressing his readers: “Parenting hits different when you work in AI.” Folks, what is the p(doom) of becoming estranged from your kid? A baby can’t understand what a father is reading it, but it can recognize his voice. There’s something perverse about some of a baby’s early and formative exposure to what its father sounds like being an AI approximation. And already wanting to automate parenting duties this early on doesn’t bode well for the future. The precious time between a child and a parent doesn’t need to be streamlined, but the AI industry is obsessed with selling us on the idea of optimizing every part of our lives. Let an AI like Meta’s buzzy Muse agent send texts and emails on your behalf. Let an AI plan out your day or plan out your vacation. Let it handle bookings and reservations.

candidates.title: Building a Space Workforce Fit for the Future
candidates.raw_excerpt: The need for a qualified and prepared talent pool is becoming one of the commercial space industry’s major challenges. Many jobs in the industry require specialized skills and years of training, and nearly 75% of companies have reported difficulty filling critical positions. Industry organizations, major companies, and government agencies are all taking steps to address this workforce challenge, resulting in 27% industry job growth over the last decade and average salaries that are double that of other private sector careers. But as organizations such as the Space Force still have 25% of their mission critical roles unfilled , it is clear that more needs to be done to build up the modern space workforce. The need to attract more workers isn’t just about filling new roles as the industry grows. The space workforce is facing a demographic time bomb as a large portion approaches retirement age without enough skilled workers to replace them. Nearly 40% of NASA’s science and engineering workforce are 55 or older. As senior employees depart, institutional knowledge and experience with legacy systems go with them. On the other end, demand from other sectors such as tech, finance, and defense for recent college graduates with strong technical skills has created a competitive labor market. The resulting labor crunch slows down growth and innovation in the space industry. The interest in space-related careers remains high thanks in large part to inspiring success such as the Artemis II mission, but traditional paths to entry, such as a college degree, require significant time and financial commitment that put it out of reach for many potential workers. candidates.title: American Airlines to Adopt Starlink for Full Mainline Fleet
candidates.raw_excerpt: American Airlines is expanding its planned rollout with SpaceX ’s Starlink for in-flight connectivity to now include its full mainline fleet of both Airbus and Boeing aircraft. The rollout, targeted to begin in early 2027, will include more than 1,000 Airbus and Boeing narrowbody and widebody aircraft. This comes after American announced plans in May to equip more than 500 Airbus aircraft in the mainline fleet with Starlink. The rollout will use the Starlink Performance Aero terminal, designed for up to 1 Gbps per terminal. “Our customers have told us that dependable connectivity can make a meaningful difference in how they spend their time in the air,” American’s Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden commented. “Starlink will give our customers countless options to make the most of their time while traveling. Just as importantly, it provides the foundation for future innovations that will further enhance the customer experience.” American currently offers free Wi-Fi across “most mainline and regional aircraft,” according to a fleet update earlier this year. The airline has worked with Viasat and Intelsat , now SES, on in-flight connectivity. This agreement does not appear to impact SES’s multi-orbit rollout on American’s Bombardier and Embraer regional fleet . Earlier this year, American confirmed that SES had installed the service on close to 500 aircraft. American Airlines did not respond to a request to comment on the Starlink adoption. Out of the “Big Three” airlines in the U.S., United has adopted Starlink across its full fleet both mainline and regional. Delta works with Viasat and Hughes and will adopt Amazon Leo on 500 aircraft beginning in 2028. Delta not working with Starlink has drawn personal jabs from SpaceX founder Elon Musk . candidates.title: The Exploration Company to Test Lunar Hopper Demonstrator in 2027
candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: The Exploration Company The Exploration Company has announced it will test a lunar hopper demonstrator called ONEIROS in the United Arab Emirates in 2027. ONEIROS is a privately funded initiative focused on validating technologies that could eventually support lower-cost access to the lunar surface. The company plans to build a one-tonne demonstrator that will use a throttleable methane-fuelled rocket engine, autonomous navigation, and hazard-avoidance systems to demonstrate the capabilities needed for controlled landings on the Moon. According to the abstract of a paper presented at the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Antalya, Türkiye, work on the project began earlier this year. Teams have already built several breadboards to reduce technical risks ahead of the planned flight demonstration next year. The decision to conduct the flight demonstration in the UAE follows a memorandum of understanding signed with the country’s national space agency to support the project and develop local testing capabilities. While no subsequent binding agreement has been announced, the abstract confirmed that testing would take place in “the UAE desert.” The Exploration Company intends to follow ONEIROS with Hilal, a demonstrator designed to validate precision landing capabilities and methane/oxygen propulsion technologies on the Moon’s surface. The company will then move ahead with its full-scale Nyx Moon lander. Beyond its lunar lander programmes, The Exploration Company is also part of a consortium selected by the European Space Agency in February 2026 to conduct a Lunar Remote Camp study . Led by the Danish firm SAGA Space Architects, the consortium is developing a concept for a deployable lunar shelter that would initially support robotic operations, with the potential to accommodate astronauts during short stays on the lunar surface. candidates.title: Chinese scientists develop nuclear optical clock
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Chinese scientists have developed a nuclear optical clock that uses the nucleus of a thorium-229 atom to keep time, marking a major advance toward a new generation of highly precise clocks.

A team led by Ding Shiqian at Tsinghua University used a specially developed continuous-wave ultraviolet laser and a tiny crystal containing thorium-229 to detect and precisely measure a transition inside the atomic nucleus. The team then locked the laser's frequency to this nuclear transition, allowing the system to operate as a nuclear optical clock.

The findings were published online in Nature on Wednesday. The Chinese team and a European team achieved nuclear optical clock operation independently at around the same time.

Today's most precise optical clocks use transitions involving electrons in atoms. A nuclear optical clock instead uses a transition inside the atomic nucleus as its timing reference. Because the nucleus is much smaller than the surrounding atom, it is less susceptible to disturbances from the external environment, potentially allowing even more precise timekeeping.

The technology could also offer advantages in size and engineering, with potential applications in satellite navigation and deep-space exploration, where highly accurate timing is essential.

A major obstacle has been the need for a continuous-wave laser with a wavelength of 148 nanometers, needed to precisely drive the thorium-229 transition. Ding's team was the first to develop such a laser.
